# Core

Core language intrinsics.

## Installation

Add `Core` to the `[Dependencies]` table of your package's `Rux.toml`:

```toml
[Dependencies]
Core = { Namespace = "Rux", Version = "0.1.0" }
```

Standard packages are declared by hand: the registry does not serve them, so `rux add Rux/Core` cannot add them.

## Guide

Core declares primitive associated constants, diagnostics, value protocols, and compile-time context.

Core is optional. Scalar types, arithmetic, arrays, inferred string literals, and range syntax work without it. Every primitive type is built into the compiler; Core extends them, and importing a primitive from Core imports its associated constants. Slice and range fields are compiler-owned. A replacement package can provide the same extensions and intrinsic declarations; the compiler assigns no privilege to the name or manifest identity of Core.

### What it provides

- **Compile-time context** — [`#target`](/docs/api/core/target#target-constant) (os, arch, abi, endian, pointer width, data model, object format, triple, `HasFeature`), [`#build`](/docs/api/core/build#build-constant), [`#compiler`](/docs/api/core/compiler#compiler-constant), [`#source`](/docs/api/core/source#source-constant), and [`#config`](/docs/api/core/config#config-constant), together with the enums they are typed by: [`OperatingSystem`](/docs/api/core/target#operating-system), [`Architecture`](/docs/api/core/target#architecture), [`ApplicationBinaryInterface`](/docs/api/core/target#application-binary-interface), [`Endianness`](/docs/api/core/target#endianness), [`DataModel`](/docs/api/core/target#data-model), [`ObjectFormat`](/docs/api/core/target#object-format), [`BuildMode`](/docs/api/core/build#build-mode), [`OptimizationMode`](/docs/api/core/build#optimization-mode), [`OutputKind`](/docs/api/core/build#output-kind), [`TargetFeature`](/docs/api/core/target#target-feature).
- **Diagnostics** — [`Assert`](/docs/api/core/diagnostics#assert), [`DebugAssert`](/docs/api/core/diagnostics#debug-assert), and [`Panic`](/docs/api/core/diagnostics#panic) report and terminate; [`#Error`](/docs/api/core/diagnostics#error) and [`#Warn`](/docs/api/core/diagnostics#warn) reject or flag an unsupported configuration while compiling and produce no runtime code. A release build removes [`DebugAssert`](/docs/api/core/diagnostics#debug-assert) checks without evaluating their arguments. Neither [`Assert`](/docs/api/core/diagnostics#assert) nor [`Panic`](/docs/api/core/diagnostics#panic) unwinds, so no destructor runs on the way out — anything that must be released on a failing path belongs to a caller that saw the failure, which is what a native fallible `T ! E` is for.
- **Native outcome questions** — [`Succeeded`](/docs/api/core/outcomes#succeeded) and [`Failed`](/docs/api/core/outcomes#failed) answer which channel a native fallible `T ! E` holds without unwrapping it. Native forms have no methods of their own, so these are ordinary generic functions; each takes the outcome by value, so a call's result is asked directly and a named outcome with a move-only payload is passed as `<-outcome`.
- **Ordering** — the result of a three-way comparison, with [`IsLess`](/docs/api/core/ordering#is-less), [`IsEqual`](/docs/api/core/ordering#is-equal), [`IsGreater`](/docs/api/core/ordering#is-greater), the derived [`IsLessOrEqual`](/docs/api/core/ordering#is-less-or-equal) and [`IsGreaterOrEqual`](/docs/api/core/ordering#is-greater-or-equal), and [`Reverse`](/docs/api/core/ordering#reverse). Absence and failure are not library types: they are the native optional `T?` and fallible `T ! E`, with the native unit `()` for an operation with nothing to report.
- **Interfaces for generic code** — [`Equatable`](/docs/api/core/equatable) and [`Comparable`](/docs/api/core/comparable) borrow their `Self`-typed operands through non-null references, [`Hashable`](/docs/api/core/hashable) gives the 64-bit summary a table keys on, and [`Iterator`](/docs/api/core/iterator)/[`Iterable`](/docs/api/core/iterable) name the iteration protocol the compiler drives by shape. Resource types prohibit copying with a bodyless canonical `=` and release themselves with `~Type`. Bounds such as `func Sort<T: Comparable>(...)` resolve `Self` to each type argument without dynamic dispatch.
- **Integer arithmetic** — [`AddChecked`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#add-checked), [`SubChecked`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#sub-checked), and [`MulChecked`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#mul-checked) report whether the true answer was representable and write the machine's answer either way; [`AddWrapping`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#add-wrapping), [`SubWrapping`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#sub-wrapping), and [`MulWrapping`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#mul-wrapping) name the wrapping that `+`, `-`, and `*` already do; [`AddSaturating`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#add-saturating), [`SubSaturating`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#sub-saturating), and [`MulSaturating`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#mul-saturating) clamp to whichever limit the true answer ran past. [`MaximumOf`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#maximum-of) and [`MinimumOf`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#minimum-of) report a type's limits. All are generic over the integer type and work at every width, signed and unsigned, deriving a type's zero, signedness, and limits from one operand rather than being written out per width. The operation comes first in each name because [`CheckedAdd`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#checked-add), [`CheckedSub`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#checked-sub), and [`CheckedMul`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#checked-mul) already name the compiler's [`uint64`](/docs/api/core/integers#uint64) intrinsics, which are emitted inline and are what allocation-size arithmetic is written with.
- **Bit operations** — [`CountOnes`](/docs/api/core/bits#count-ones), [`CountZeros`](/docs/api/core/bits#count-zeros), [`LeadingZeros`](/docs/api/core/bits#leading-zeros), [`TrailingZeros`](/docs/api/core/bits#trailing-zeros), [`LeadingOnes`](/docs/api/core/bits#leading-ones), [`TrailingOnes`](/docs/api/core/bits#trailing-ones), [`RotateLeft`](/docs/api/core/bits#rotate-left), [`RotateRight`](/docs/api/core/bits#rotate-right), [`ReverseBits`](/docs/api/core/bits#reverse-bits), [`ReverseBytes`](/docs/api/core/bits#reverse-bytes), [`BitAt`](/docs/api/core/bits#bit-at), [`BitWidthOf`](/docs/api/core/bits#bit-width-of), [`IsPowerOfTwo`](/docs/api/core/bits#is-power-of-two), and [`ShiftRightLogical`](/docs/api/core/bits#shift-right-logical). All are generic over the integer type and right at every width, signed and unsigned: `>>` copies the sign bit down on a signed type, so everything that reads a value's bits as bits goes through [`ShiftRightLogical`](/docs/api/core/bits#shift-right-logical), which brings zeros in either way.
- **Byte order** — [`ToLittleEndian`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#to-little-endian), [`FromLittleEndian`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#from-little-endian), [`ToBigEndian`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#to-big-endian), and [`FromBigEndian`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#from-big-endian) convert a value already in a register; [`StoreLittleEndian`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#store-little-endian), [`StoreBigEndian`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#store-big-endian), [`LoadLittleEndian`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#load-little-endian), and [`LoadBigEndian`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#load-big-endian) move one through raw bytes at any alignment, which is what a file or wire format needs. [`TargetIsLittleEndian`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#target-is-little-endian) reports this target's own order, established from its storage rather than from a list of known targets.
- **Checked conversion** — [`ConvertChecked`](/docs/api/core/conversion#convert-checked) reports whether a primitive value survived the conversion and writes the machine's answer either way; [`ConvertWrapping`](/docs/api/core/conversion#convert-wrapping) names the wrapping `as` already does, and [`ConvertSaturating`](/docs/api/core/conversion#convert-saturating) clamps to the destination's range. Every check is a round trip in the source type, plus one test for the pair a round trip cannot see — a value and its conversion that disagree in sign, which is how `-1` reaches [`uint64`](/docs/api/core/integers#uint64). [`IsSignedType`](/docs/api/core/conversion#is-signed-type) reports whether a type has values below zero.
- **Float classification** — [`IsNaN`](/docs/api/core/float-classification#is-nan), [`IsZero`](/docs/api/core/float-classification#is-zero), [`IsInfinite`](/docs/api/core/float-classification#is-infinite), [`IsFinite`](/docs/api/core/float-classification#is-finite), [`IsNegativeZero`](/docs/api/core/float-classification#is-negative-zero), [`IsSignNegative`](/docs/api/core/float-classification#is-sign-negative), [`IsSignPositive`](/docs/api/core/float-classification#is-sign-positive), and [`SignOf`](/docs/api/core/float-classification#sign-of). All are arithmetic rather than bit inspection, so one implementation serves every float width including the software-lowered ones, whose storage carries padding no generic function could locate a sign bit inside of. The sign of a zero, which comparison cannot see, is read from the infinity it divides into.
- **Primitive associated constants** — `Bits`, `Bytes`, `Min`, `Max` and the floating-point set (`Lowest`, `MinPositive`, `Epsilon`, `Infinity`, `NaN`) for every integer width and every character width from [`char8`](/docs/api/core/characters#char8) to [`char512`](/docs/api/core/characters#char512), width metadata for every boolean width from [`bool8`](/docs/api/core/booleans#bool8) to [`bool512`](/docs/api/core/booleans#bool512), and the finite and special constant set for every float width from [`float8`](/docs/api/core/floating-point#float8) to [`float512`](/docs/api/core/floating-point#float512). The scalar widths from [`char32`](/docs/api/core/characters#char32) to [`char512`](/docs/api/core/characters#char512) share one range, U+0000 to U+10FFFF, however many bytes they occupy. The string widths expose none: a string is a view over code units rather than a value with a width, so a width or a limit would describe neither it nor the units.

### Primitive constants and imports

```rux
import Core::int8;

func Main() -> int {
    let minimum = int8::Min;
    let message: char8[..] = "hello";
    return message.length as int + minimum as int;
}
```

[`int8`](/docs/api/core/integers#int8) is built into the compiler, so it names the scalar type without an import; `import Core::int8;` imports Core's `extend int8` block, which is what makes [`int8::Min`](/docs/api/core/integers#int8-min) available. The built-in aliases import their canonical widths: `import Core::byte;` gives `byte::Max`, the same constant as [`uint8::Max`](/docs/api/core/integers#uint8-max), and `import Core::bool;` gives `bool::Bits`. Loading a dependency that imports it does not import its APIs into the caller. The same rule applies between source files.

Core declares no primitive type: each primitive file holds one documented `extend` block. Core defines integer and character limits, width metadata, and finite floating constants using ordinary constant expressions. Native integer metadata uses `sizeof`, so it follows the compilation target. The float limits of [`float8`](/docs/api/core/floating-point#float8) and [`float16`](/docs/api/core/floating-point#float16) are literals — [`float8`](/docs/api/core/floating-point#float8), the E4M3 format, tops out at 240 and [`float16`](/docs/api/core/floating-point#float16) at 65504 — while `Infinity` and `NaN` at every width, and every limit of [`float80`](/docs/api/core/floating-point#float80), [`float128`](/docs/api/core/floating-point#float128), [`float256`](/docs/api/core/floating-point#float256) and [`float512`](/docs/api/core/floating-point#float512), are bodyless `intrinsic const` declarations whose values the compiler supplies from the format itself.

### Sequence views and ranges

The language supplies read-only `T[..]` and writable `var T[..]` views. Neither annotation needs a Core import. Their `.data` and `.length` fields are compiler-owned. A view owns no storage, and copying it copies two words. Its backing storage must remain alive while it is used.

```rux
func Sum(values: int[..]) -> int {
    var total = 0;
    for value in values { total += value; }
    return total;
}

func Fill(values: var int[..], value: int) {
    for index in 0..values.length { values[index] = value; }
}

func Main() -> int {
    var storage: int[3] = [1, 2, 3];
    let view = storage[..];
    Fill(view, 4);
    return Sum(view) - 12;
}
```

A writable view weakens to a read-only one implicitly; a read-only view cannot be strengthened. Binding a view with `let` does not freeze its pointee. `[]` constructs an empty view when a slice type is expected. Use `pointer[..length]` to view raw storage, and `view[start..end]` to select a subview. Pointer ranges require an end because pointers carry no length. These operations use element counts rather than byte counts.

Ranges are written `int..int`, `int..=int`, `int..`, `..int`, `..=int`, and `..` in annotations. Their `.start` and `.end` fields exist only when the corresponding bound exists, with no declaration or import required.

Literal text is `char8[..]`, `char16[..]`, or `char32[..]`; the prefixes are `c8`, `c16`, and `c32`, and an unprefixed literal uses UTF-8. The descriptor length counts code units, excluding the trailing NUL in literal storage. Text can be passed directly to a function taking the corresponding read-only character slice. Slicing can split an encoded scalar, so validated-text operations belong in Text and Unicode. A literal cannot become a writable view.

Core diagnostic messages and compile-time context text use `char8[..]`. External functions taking raw pointers receive `"literal".data`. Concrete slice extensions can add methods for one element type; reusable generic algorithms use ordinary generic functions.

### Ownership and borrowing

Core methods borrow ordinary values with `&T` and mutable receivers with `&var T`; callers pass the value directly and the compiler creates the short-lived borrow. Named move-only values require `<-` when ownership crosses a binding, call, assignment, return, or consuming receiver. Copyable Core values use generated structural copying. Canonical constructors are type calls such as `SemanticVersion(1, 2, 3)`, and descriptive factories retain their names.

Raw pointers remain where absence, storage, or address arithmetic is part of the contract: slice fields, nullable `TryInto*` outputs, unchecked checked-arithmetic/conversion destinations, byte-order buffers, and zeroization.

[`Assert`](/docs/api/core/diagnostics#assert) and [`Panic`](/docs/api/core/diagnostics#panic) failures have the same UTF-8, LF-terminated layout on every supported target:

```text
Assertion failed: message
  at Function (path:line:column)
```

[`Panic`](/docs/api/core/diagnostics#panic) uses `Panic: message` on the first line. The location uses a package-relative path when the source belongs to the package root, and qualified method or module names are retained.

### Example

```rux
import Core::{ #target, #Error };

when #target.os {
    .Windows, .Linux, .macOS, .FreeBSD => {},
    else => #Error("Unsupported operating system")
}
```

```rux
import Core::{ Assert, SemanticVersion };

func Major(version: &SemanticVersion) -> uint {
    return version.major;
}

func Main() -> int {
    let version = SemanticVersion(1, 2, 3);
    let answer: int32? = .Some(42i32);
    Assert(Major(version) == 1u, "borrowed version");
    Assert((answer ?? 0i32) == 42i32, "present optional value");
    return 0;
}
```

| [`ReverseBits<T>`](/docs/api/core/bits#reverse-bits)                          | The value with its bits in the opposite order: bit zero becomes the highest bit and back again.            |
| [`ReverseBytes<T>`](/docs/api/core/bits#reverse-bytes)                        | The value with its bytes in the opposite order, leaving the bits within each byte where they were.         |
| [`IsPowerOfTwo<T>`](/docs/api/core/bits#is-power-of-two)                      | Whether the value has exactly one bit set.                                                                 |
| [`CheckedAdd`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#checked-add)                         | Adds two unsigned 64-bit values and reports whether the true sum is representable.                         |
| [`CheckedSub`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#checked-sub)                         | Subtracts one unsigned 64-bit value from another and reports whether the true difference is representable. |
| [`CheckedMul`](/docs/api/core/arithmetic#checked-mul)                         | Multiplies two unsigned 64-bit values and reports whether the true product is representable.               |
| [`IsSignedType<T>`](/docs/api/core/conversion#is-signed-type)                 | Whether the integer type of `sample` has values below zero.                                                |
| [`ConvertChecked<From, To>`](/docs/api/core/conversion#convert-checked)       | Converts a primitive value to another primitive type and reports whether the true value was representable. |
| [`ConvertWrapping<From, To>`](/docs/api/core/conversion#convert-wrapping)     | Converts a primitive value to another primitive type, keeping whatever fits.                               |
| [`ConvertSaturating<From, To>`](/docs/api/core/conversion#convert-saturating) | Converts a primitive value to an integer type, clamping to that type's range instead of wrapping.          |
| [`Assert`](/docs/api/core/diagnostics#assert)                                 | Terminates the program unless `condition` holds.                                                           |
| [`DebugAssert`](/docs/api/core/diagnostics#debug-assert)                      | Terminates the program unless `condition` holds, in builds that keep debug assertions.                     |
| [`Panic`](/docs/api/core/diagnostics#panic)                                   | Terminates the program, reporting `message`.                                                               |
| [`#Error`](/docs/api/core/diagnostics#error)                                  | Rejects the build where it is written, reporting `message`.                                                |
| [`#Warn`](/docs/api/core/diagnostics#warn)                                    | Reports `message` as a compilation warning where it is written, without rejecting the build.               |
| [`TargetIsLittleEndian`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#target-is-little-endian)   | Whether this target stores an integer's least significant byte first.                                      |
| [`ToLittleEndian<T>`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#to-little-endian)             | The value's bytes as a little-endian value would hold them.                                                |
| [`FromLittleEndian<T>`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#from-little-endian)         | The value a little-endian bit pattern stands for on this target.                                           |
| [`ToBigEndian<T>`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#to-big-endian)                   | The value's bytes as a big-endian value would hold them.                                                   |
| [`FromBigEndian<T>`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#from-big-endian)               | The value a big-endian bit pattern stands for on this target.                                              |
| [`StoreLittleEndian<T>`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#store-little-endian)       | Writes an integer to raw bytes, least significant byte first.                                              |
| [`StoreBigEndian<T>`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#store-big-endian)             | Writes an integer to raw bytes, most significant byte first.                                               |
| [`LoadLittleEndian<T>`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#load-little-endian)         | Reads an integer from raw bytes holding it least significant byte first.                                   |
| [`LoadBigEndian<T>`](/docs/api/core/byte-order#load-big-endian)               | Reads an integer from raw bytes holding it most significant byte first.                                    |
| [`IsNaN<T>`](/docs/api/core/float-classification#is-nan)                      | Whether the value is not a number.                                                                         |
| [`IsZero<T>`](/docs/api/core/float-classification#is-zero)                    | Whether the value is either zero.                                                                          |
| [`IsInfinite<T>`](/docs/api/core/float-classification#is-infinite)            | Whether the value is an infinity, of either sign.                                                          |
| [`IsFinite<T>`](/docs/api/core/float-classification#is-finite)                | Whether the value is an ordinary number: neither a NaN nor an infinity.                                    |
| [`IsNegativeZero<T>`](/docs/api/core/float-classification#is-negative-zero)   | Whether the value is the zero that carries a minus sign.                                                   |
| [`IsSignNegative<T>`](/docs/api/core/float-classification#is-sign-negative)   | Whether the value carries a minus sign.                                                                    |
| [`IsSignPositive<T>`](/docs/api/core/float-classification#is-sign-positive)   | Whether the value carries a plus sign.                                                                     |
| [`SignOf<T>`](/docs/api/core/float-classification#sign-of)                    | The value's sign as one of `-1`, `+1`, or the zero it started from.                                        |
| [`Succeeded<T, E>`](/docs/api/core/outcomes#succeeded)                        | Whether `outcome` holds a success.                                                                         |
| [`Failed<T, E>`](/docs/api/core/outcomes#failed)                              | Whether `outcome` holds a failure.                                                                         |
| [`Zeroize`](/docs/api/core/zeroize)                                           | Overwrites a byte range with zeros, and is never removed however unread those bytes are afterwards.        |
